Re:  2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed 
Rule (CMS-0062-P): Comments of HealthLX 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
HealthLX appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards 
and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P), published in the Federal 
Register on April 14, 2026. We are a health information technology vendor that provides 
interoperability and prior authorization services to health plans, supporting their compliance with 
the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), the CMS Interoperability 
and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), and the Contract Year 2026 Medicare 
Advantage and Part D final rule (CMS-4208-F). We build and operate FHIRÂ®-based APIs, 
supporting infrastructure, and prior authorization workflows that impacted payers rely on to meet 
these requirements today. 
We are in strong support of the overall direction of this proposed rule. Extending electronic 
prior authorization to drugs, adopting FHIR standards under HIPAA, requiring payers to report 
their API endpoints to a centralized location, and aligning standards versioning with the ONC 
Health IT Certification Program are all measures that will reduce administrative burden, 
accelerate patient access to care, and strengthen the interoperability ecosystem CMS has built 
over the last several rulemakings. Our comments below are offered in that spirit: we support the 
proposals and, drawing on our direct implementation experience, we offer specific 
recommendations to help CMS make them work in practice. 
Our comments are organized to follow the structure of the proposed rule and respond to several 
of the specific Requests for Comment (RFCs) where our perspective as an implementer is most 
useful. 
Before turning to the specific proposals, we offer one overarching recommendation: that CMS 
use the final rule to articulate a clear, unifying vision for how this rulemaking fits within the 
broader interoperability framework CMS has assembled, including the CMS Interoperability and 
Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final 
Rule (CMS-0057-F), the Contract Year 2026 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule

(CMS-4208-F), the ONC Health IT Certification Program and the standards adopted at 45 CFR 
170.215, HIPAA Administrative Simplification, and emerging national infrastructure such as 
TEFCA and the National Directory of Healthcare Providers & Services. Implementers today 
must infer the intended end state from a sequence of separate rules; a stated architectural 
vision, together with a clear statement of how these requirements align, sequence, and avoid 
conflict, would let payers and vendors plan investments coherently, avoid building to approaches 
that are about to be superseded, and reduce the duplicative or contradictory obligations that 
arise when related mandates are read in isolation. Several of our recommendations below are 
aimed at exactly these seams between rules, and we return to this theme in our conclusion. 
1.  Interoperability Standards and Implementation Guides (Section II.A) 
1.1  Streamlining required standards and use-case-specific IGs (Section II.A.3) 
CMS asks whether requiring both the base FHIR standard and the use-case-specific IGs (e.g., 
CRD, DTR, and PAS for the Prior Authorization API) is necessary, or whether requiring the IGs 
alone would provide comparable technical guidance while reducing regulatory complexity. We 
recommend that CMS require the use-case-specific IGs and treat the base FHIR standard 
as incorporated by reference through those IGs. 
In practice, every Da Vinci IG already constrains and builds upon a specific version of base 
FHIR; conformance to CRD, DTR, and PAS necessarily entails conformance to the underlying 
FHIR release the IG is built on. Independently naming both creates two avoidable risks for 
implementers: (1) version drift, where the separately cited base standard advances to a version 
the IG has not yet been re-published against, forcing payers to reconcile conflicting normative 
requirements; and (2) ambiguity about which document controls when they differ. Requiring the 
IGs and letting them carry the base-version dependency eliminates both problems. Where CMS 
believes an API has a genuine need beyond what its IGs constrain, we encourage CMS to 
name that gap explicitly rather than requiring the full base standard by default. 
1.2  Specifying relevant IG capabilities to reduce unnecessary development (Section 
II.A.3) 
We support CMS's proposal to identify only the capabilities of an IG relevant to a given API use 
case, such as scoping the SMART App Launch IG to the â€œPatient Access for Standalone Appsâ€ 
capability set for the Patient Access API. Open-ended conformance to an entire IG forces 
implementers to build and test capabilities that no production use case exercises, which adds 
cost without adding patient or provider value. We encourage CMS to extend this 
capability-scoping approach across all of the required IGs and to publish the specific capability 
sets in sub-regulatory guidance so they can be refreshed as the IGs mature. 
1.3  FAST Security IG and Tiered OAuth, readiness for B2B authorization at scale 
(Section II.A.5) 
CMS recommends, but does not require, the HL7 FAST Security IG and asks how it would know 
when the IG is ready to be required and how much testing is necessary. We agree that the 
FAST Security IG addresses a real and growing problem: today, payer-to-payer and 
provider-access authorization relies heavily on bespoke, bilaterally negotiated trust relationships 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹

and manual registration, which do not scale as the number of connections grows 
combinatorially. The UDAP-based dynamic client registration and trust-community model in the 
FAST Security IG is the right long-term direction. 
That said, we recommend CMS continue to recommend rather than require the FAST 
Security IG in this rulemaking, and signal a clear intent to require it in a future rule once 
readiness conditions are met. Specifically, we suggest CMS look for: (1) a critical mass of 
production, not pilot, deployments across payers and EHRs; (2) one or more operational trust 
communities with published, audited certificate policies that impacted payers can actually join; 
and (3) successful results from a structured connectathon-style testing program (e.g., HL7 FHIR 
Connectathons and/or ONC-coordinated testing) demonstrating cross-vendor interoperability. 
On Tiered OAuth, we support recommending it for the Patient Access API first, where the 
end-user authentication problem is most acute, before considering it for the system-to-system 
APIs. 
To the second question, whether trust communities exist today, we note that frameworks such 
as TEFCA/QHIN trust infrastructure and existing UDAP trust communities are emerging but are 
not yet uniformly available to all impacted payers. CMS can accelerate readiness by funding 
and endorsing a reference trust community and conformance test suite rather than leaving each 
payer and vendor to solve B2B trust independently. 
1.4  CDex IG: recommend now, require after real-world testing (Sections II.A.5 and 
II.H) 
CMS asks (in the HIPAA context) whether the Da Vinci CDex IG should be adopted as the 
attachments standard or merely recommended to give industry time to test it. We recommend 
CMS recommend, but not yet mandate, the CDex IG for prior authorization attachments at 
this time, with a stated intent to require it in a subsequent rule. 
CDex is the correct architectural choice for attachments because it lets payers request precisely 
the documentation they need and lets providers respond without over-sharing, which is a 
meaningful burden reduction over today's fax-and-portal practice. However, CDex production 
maturity across payer and EHR systems lags that of CRD, DTR, and PAS. Mandating CDex on 
the same compliance timeline as the core PAS workflow risks making the entire prior 
authorization transaction dependent on the least-mature component. If CMS does adopt CDex 
now, we strongly urge a later, phased compliance date for CDex than for the core FHIR prior 
authorization transaction standards, so that payers can deploy the PAS workflow first and layer 
in structured attachments as the IG matures. 
1.5  CARIN RTPBC and real-time pharmacy cost in the Patient Access API, 
recommend RTPBC IG for patient access (Section II.A.5) 
There is genuine patient value in surfacing real-time prescription cost and coverage information, 
and demand for it is well established in consumer-facing pharmacy tools. We see the CARIN 
Consumer RTPBC IG and the PDex US Drug Formulary IG as complementary rather than 
overlapping: the PDex Drug Formulary IG describes formulary structure and coverage at a 
plan/group level, while RTPBC returns a patient-specific, real-time benefit and price quote. They 
answer different questions. We would support CMS recommending the RTPBC IG for the 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹
Page 3 of 13 
Patient Access API as a next step, while acknowledging that patient-specific real-time pricing 
depends on PBM data feeds that not all payers control directly; CMS should account for that 
dependency in any future requirement and in burden estimates. 
2.  NCPDP Standards for Pharmacy-Benefit Drugs (Section II.A.2) 
We support requiring the NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary & Benefit (F&B), and Real-Time 
Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standards to align electronic prior authorization of pharmacy-benefit 
drugs across CMS programs with existing Medicare Part D practice. We note that the scope is 
appropriately targeted: MA organizations are already required to support all three standards, so 
the proposal extends a proven baseline to Medicaid/CHIP FFS, managed care, and FFE QHP 
issuers rather than inventing a new obligation. On CMS's question of whether requiring both the 
F&B and RTPB standards adds value or creates duplicative burden: 
â€¢â€‹
The two standards serve distinct functions and we recommend retaining both. The F&B 
standard provides a comprehensive, cacheable view of formulary structure and 
prior-authorization indicators suitable for bulk loading into EHRs and decision-support 
tooling; the RTPB standard provides a real-time, patient-specific coverage and cost 
response at the point of prescribing. RTPB does not fully replace the population-level 
discoverability that F&B provides, and F&B alone cannot deliver patient-specific real-time 
accuracy. 
â€¢â€‹
On F&B currency: in our experience, the lag between a payer/PBM formulary policy 
change and its reflection in the published F&B flat file is a recurring source of provider 
abrasion and inappropriate prior-authorization triggers. We recommend CMS set an 
expectation for maximum F&B update latency (for example, no less frequently than 
weekly, and promptly following any change to a prior-authorization-required indicator) 
rather than leaving cadence undefined. 
On the Da Vinci CRD â€œCoverageInformationâ€ extension: yes, the CRD IG is technically capable 
of returning specific coverage information, including whether prior authorization is required and 
which pathway (medical vs. pharmacy benefit) applies, through that extension. We believe the 
cleanest design is to use the CRD CoverageInformation response to signal to the provider's 
system whether a given drug should be routed to the FHIR Prior Authorization API (medical 
benefit) or to the NCPDP pathway (pharmacy benefit), so the provider does not have to guess. 
We would welcome the opportunity to contribute implementation detail on this routing pattern to 
any CMS or HL7 guidance. 
3.  Incorporating Medical-Benefit Drugs into the Prior Authorization API 
(Section II.B.3) 
We support incorporating coverage and documentation requirements for medical-benefit drugs 
into the existing Prior Authorization API. Reusing the CRD/DTR/PAS workflow already being 
built for non-drug items and services for medical-benefit drugs is the right approach: it avoids a 
parallel infrastructure and lets payers and providers extend a workflow they are already 
implementing under CMS-0057-F. 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹

On CMS's question about the rubric for categorizing a drug as medical-benefit (Prior 
Authorization API) versus pharmacy-benefit (NCPDP): using the claims-adjudication system 
through which the drug is processed is a workable and objective default for most payers, and 
we support it as the primary rule. However, edge cases exist. The same drug can be 
adjudicated under either benefit depending on site of care or plan design. We therefore 
recommend CMS (1) pair the claims-system rubric with a machine-readable signal (the CRD 
CoverageInformation extension discussed above) so the provider's system is told the correct 
pathway at the point of need, rather than inferring it, and (2) confirm in guidance that a drug may 
legitimately appear under both pathways for different scenarios without that constituting 
non-compliance. 
4.  Reporting Payer API Endpoints to CMS (Section II.E) 
We strongly support requiring impacted payers to report their interoperability API endpoints and 
associated technical documentation to CMS for publication in a centralized location. Endpoint 
discovery is one of the largest practical barriers to interoperability today. As a vendor that 
connects to many payers on behalf of providers and patients, we routinely spend significant 
effort simply locating a given payer's endpoint, capability statement, and registration process. A 
reliable central directory directly reduces that friction and accelerates real data flow. 
We offer the following recommendations on implementation: 
â€¢â€‹
Adopt the FHIR-enabled approach. In response to CMS's question about a 
machine-readable file versus a FHIR-enabled registry: we strongly favor a FHIR-enabled 
registry built on the Endpoint and related resources. A FHIR registry allows automated, 
programmatic consumption by app developers, EHRs, and payer systems; supports 
validation at submission time; and enables incremental updates rather than 
re-publication of a static file. A flat machine-readable file should at most be a transitional 
artifact, not the end state. 
â€¢â€‹
Align with the NDH Endpoint Profile (the alternative proposal). We support CMS's 
alternative proposal to align reporting with the National Directory of Healthcare Providers 
& Services (NDH) IG Endpoint Profile resources. Reusing an existing, 
industry-developed profile reduces payer reporting burden and developer integration 
burden by giving both sides a single, standardized representation rather than a 
CMS-specific schema. 
â€¢â€‹
Avoid duplicative data elements. Collecting a separate direct URL to each FHIR 
capability statement is largely duplicative: the FHIR specification already requires the 
capability statement to be available at [base]/metadata. Requiring the base endpoint is 
sufficient; CMS can derive or fetch the capability statement from it. We recommend 
dropping the separately reported capability-statement URL field to reduce burden and 
the risk of the two fields falling out of sync. To be clear, we are not suggesting that 
payers stop publishing FHIR capability statements. Those remain essential to discovery 
and would continue to be available at [base]/metadata. We recommend eliminating only 
the redundant, separately reported URL, not the capability statement itself, so that 
existing discovery flows that rely on capability statements are unaffected. 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹

â€¢â€‹
Collect discrete, structured auth details. To facilitate faster integration, we 
recommend CMS collect the specific authorization/authentication protocol (e.g., 
SMART/OAuth flavor, UDAP support) as a discrete, coded field rather than only as 
free-text documentation URLs. Discrete fields let developer tooling auto-configure 
connections; documentation URLs still require a human to read them. Such a discrete 
field could also contain an â€œotherâ€ category as a catch-all so as not to restrict valid 
responses. 
On the proposed update cadence (reporting within 60 days of the effective date, updating within 
one week of any change, and annual verification), we agree with the overall structure but 
recommend two adjustments grounded in operational experience. First, we recommend 
extending the initial reporting window from 60 to 90 days, which better reflects the time 
impacted payers need to assemble and validate endpoint, capability, and authorization details 
across their delegated entities and vendors before first publication. Second, we recommend 
easing the one-week update obligation for payers that have not yet automated reporting: a 
one-week deadline is readily achievable through a FHIR-enabled registry with programmatic 
update, but is burdensome to meet through manual submission, so we suggest CMS allow a 
longer window (for example, 30 days) for manually reported changes, converging on the 
one-week timeframe as automated, FHIR-based updating becomes available. Annual 
verification is reasonable as proposed. 
5.  Access APIs and Usage Metrics (Section II.F) 
We support adding prior-authorization data for drugs to the Patient Access, Provider Access, 
and Payer-to-Payer APIs (II.F.1). Consistent, comprehensive prior-authorization information 
across these APIs improves care coordination and reduces redundant requests, and reusing the 
data categories already defined for non-drug items keeps the implementation tractable. 
We also support the new Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization API usage 
metrics (II.F.2.c). Usage data is essential to understanding whether these APIs are actually 
being adopted, and it will help CMS and the industry target the real adoption gaps. We want to 
highlight one proposed metric in particular as especially valuable: the percentage of all prior 
authorization requests received through the Prior Authorization API. This is the single most 
important adoption signal in the rule. It directly measures the share of prior authorization volume 
moving through the modern FHIR pathway versus legacy fax and portal channels. We strongly 
encourage CMS to retain it, and we note in Section 10 below how it can anchor CMS's 
API-oversight strategy. 
On the mechanism for states and payers to report these metrics: in response to CMS's RFC, we 
recommend supporting a FHIR-based, automated reporting path (e.g., a measure/report 
submission to a CMS FHIR endpoint) as an alternative to portal or form entry. Automated 
submission reduces burden, reduces transcription error, and is consistent with the FHIR-first 
direction of the rest of the rule. As a transitional accommodation, a portal or form-based path 
should remain available for small health plans and other payers that cannot yet automate, with 
the expectation that they migrate to automated, FHIR-based submission as their capabilities 
mature. 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹
Page 6 of 13 
On the public prior-authorization metrics (II.C.6 and II.C.7), we support reporting numeric counts 
in addition to percentages, and we support the new drug metrics, including average and median 
decision time and the â€œremain denied after appealâ€ metrics, which give patients and providers a 
far more complete picture than percentages alone. One caution from an implementer's 
standpoint: these usage and outcome metrics measure volume and outcomes but not technical 
conformance. A payer can post strong usage numbers while still exposing an API that behaves 
inconsistently for the apps and EHRs that consume it. We therefore urge CMS to treat these 
metrics as complementary to, not a substitute for, the conformance-testing approach we 
recommend in Section 10. 
6.  Standards Versioning and Expiration (Sections II.A, II.H.11, II.J) 
We strongly support CMS's proposal to cross-reference standards versions adopted by the 
Secretary in 45 CFR 170.215 (including the versions adopted through the ONC HTI-4 final rule 
and the updated versions in 170.215(j), (k), (m), and (n) that ONC proposes to adopt here), and 
to let impacted payers move to newer ONC-approved versions without additional CMS 
rulemaking (subject to the stated conditions on legality, ONC approval, and non-disruption of 
end-user access). This is one of the most important structural improvements in the rule. Today, 
the gap between a standard maturing and a rule permitting its use creates years of unnecessary 
lag; the cross-reference approach largely closes that gap and lets implementers keep pace with 
the IGs as they improve. 
Relatedly, we support HHS relying on the HL7 Major.Minor.Patch versioning convention (II.H.11) 
so that maintenance-level updates (patch and minor releases that do not introduce breaking 
changes) do not require new rulemaking. We encourage CMS to state clearly in the final rule 
that conformance to a later compatible Minor.Patch version of a named IG satisfies the 
requirement, which removes ambiguity for implementers. 
On the proposed January 1, 2028 expiration dates for older standard versions (II.J.7), and the 
alternative of removing and replacing versions with no transition period: we urge CMS to retain 
a transition period during which both the expiring and the new versions are permitted, 
and to oppose the no-transition alternative. Real deployments and the third-party apps, 
provider EHRs, and downstream systems that consume these APIs cannot all migrate 
atomically on a single date. A defined overlap window is what makes a version transition safe; a 
hard cutover with no overlap would risk breaking live patient and provider connections. We 
believe roughly the proposed overlap (through the expiration date) is appropriate, provided the 
expiration date gives at least 12â€“18 months of overlap from the final rule's effective date. 
7.  HIPAA Adoption of FHIR for Prior Authorization Transactions (Section 
II.H) 
We support HHS adopting the FHIR standard and the CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation 
guides for prior-authorization-related â€œreferral certification and authorizationâ€ and â€œeligibilityâ€ 
transactions under HIPAA Administrative Simplification. Aligning the HIPAA transaction 
standards with the FHIR-based APIs CMS already requires of payers is essential; without it, 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹
Page 7 of 13 
payers and providers would be caught between an X12-based HIPAA mandate and a 
FHIR-based API mandate for the same business function. 
We support adopting the FHIR standard for the prior-authorization-related transactions 
specifically, namely the â€œreferral certification and authorizationâ€ (X12N 278) function and the 
narrow subset of eligibility (X12N 270/271) used to determine whether prior authorization is 
required, consistent with the scope CMS has proposed. We do not, however, support extending 
this to a wholesale replacement of the X12N 270/271 standard. The eligibility transaction serves 
many purposes well beyond prior authorization and is among the most deeply embedded, 
highest-volume transactions in healthcare, and the FHIR-based coverage-checking ecosystem 
is not yet mature enough to replace it across all use cases. We therefore support CMS's 
proposal to retain X12N 270/271 for all non-prior-authorization eligibility transactions, and we 
encourage CMS to preserve a generous coexistence period rather than deprecating established 
X12 transactions before the FHIR equivalents have proven production-ready at scale. As for the 
broader alternative of converting all referral certification and authorization transactions to FHIR, 
we believe that step is premature and would defer it to a future rulemaking once real-world 
experience with the prior-authorization-scoped transactions is in hand. 
On the direct data entry (portal) exception in 45 CFR 162.923(b) (II.H.11): we support CMS 
revisiting this exception over time. The portal exception is a significant reason fully electronic, 
standards-based prior authorization has not displaced manual workflows. It lets covered entities 
satisfy their obligations through web portals that are not interoperable and that shift burden onto 
providers' staff. We recommend CMS not remove the exception abruptly, but instead signal a 
phase-down tied to demonstrated availability and maturity of the FHIR-based transaction, with 
particular attention to small and rural practices that may need additional time and support. 
8.  Compliance Timelines and Feasibility 
Most of the API and prior-authorization proposals carry an October 1, 2027 compliance date, 
and the HIPAA FHIR standards carry a 24-month (36-month for small health plans) timeline from 
the final rule's effective date. As the vendor building these capabilities, we offer the following 
candid assessment: 
â€¢â€‹
The October 1, 2027 date is achievable for proposals that extend an existing 
CMS-0057-F workflow, such as adding medical-benefit drugs to the Prior Authorization 
API and adding drug PA data to the Access APIs, provided the final rule is published 
with enough lead time. These build on infrastructure payers are already standing up. 
The risk is not the incremental drug scope; it is compression if the final rule slips. 
â€¢â€‹
Components that depend on less-mature IGs (CDex attachments, FAST Security) need 
either a later compliance date or recommended-not-required status, as discussed in 
Sections 1.3 and 1.4. Tying a hard 2027 date to the least-mature components is the 
principal feasibility risk in the rule. 
â€¢â€‹
We support the longer HIPAA timeline (24/36 months) for the FHIR transaction 
standards, which appropriately reflects that HIPAA covered entities include providers and 
clearinghouses that are earlier in their FHIR journey than impacted payers. 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹

â€¢â€‹
For the FF-SHOP small group QHP proposals (II.D), CMS's premise, that these issuers 
already operate individual-market QHP APIs on the FFEs and can extend them, is 
generally sound, and the January 1, 2028 dates provide reasonable runway. We agree 
these issuers can largely reuse their existing implementations. 
9.  Cross-Cutting Implementation Considerations for Impacted Payers 
Several themes recur across the proposals above and, in our experience supporting payers 
under CMS-9115-F and CMS-0057-F, will largely determine whether the rule's goals are realized 
in production. Because they cut across multiple sections rather than attaching to any single 
proposal, we address them together here. 
Accountability for compliance, dependence on delegated entities and PBMs. Impacted 
payers are accountable for compliance, yet many of the transactions and much of the data the 
rule reaches, particularly for pharmacy-benefit drugs, are executed by PBMs and other 
delegated entities that the payer does not directly control. A payer may be fully prepared to 
expose the CRD, DTR, and PAS APIs or the NCPDP transactions and still be unable to comply 
if its PBM cannot support those interfaces on the same timeline. We ask CMS to (1) confirm that 
a payer may satisfy its obligations through delegated entities and vendors acting on its behalf, 
so the accountability model matches how the market actually operates; (2) make clear that the 
entities holding the data, including PBMs, are expected to support the standards the rule 
requires, rather than placing the full burden on the plans that depend on them; and (3) provide a 
reasonable accommodation, or a phased expectation, where a payer can demonstrate that a 
compliance gap is attributable to a delegated entity that is not yet ready, so that plans are not 
penalized for gaps they cannot unilaterally close. 
The role of vendors and intermediaries. Much of the infrastructure this rule contemplates is 
built and operated by technology vendors and intermediaries on payers' behalf; we are one such 
vendor. We encourage CMS to acknowledge this model explicitly, both that compliance may be 
achieved through vendors acting for a payer, and that the endpoint directory, conformance 
testing, and reporting mechanisms should accommodate vendor-operated and shared 
infrastructure rather than assuming every payer builds and runs its own technology stack. 
Recognizing this model lets payers meet the rule's requirements at the speed it demands by 
drawing on shared vendor infrastructure, rather than being pushed to build out their own 
technology stack simply to comply. 
Reporting burden and the overhead of cross-entity data coordination. Reporting 
obligations run to the payer, but the data needed to satisfy them frequently originates across 
PBMs, delegated entities, and vendors. Assembling complete, accurate metrics, particularly the 
prior-authorization and API-usage metrics in Section II.F, requires the payer to collect and 
reconcile data from systems it does not operate, and that coordination is a real and recurring 
source of overhead. We recommend CMS mitigate it by (1) confirming that reporting 
responsibility runs through the payer while making clear that contributing entities are expected 
to furnish the underlying data; (2) defining each metric precisely enough that it can be computed 
from data the payer can actually obtain, avoiding definitions that depend on information no party 
reliably holds; (3) supporting the FHIR-based automated submission path described in Section

5, which materially reduces coordination cost; and (4) permitting aggregated submission 
through a vendor or other agent acting for the payer. 
Support for small health plans. Small health plans face the same requirements with a fraction 
of the technical resources, and they are the most dependent on PBMs, vendors, and delegated 
entities for the capabilities the rule requires. We support the accommodations already in the 
proposal (the longer 36-month HIPAA timeline for small plans and the availability of a portal or 
form-based reporting path) and we encourage CMS to go further by (1) keeping the 
least-mature components (CDex, FAST Security) recommended rather than required, which 
disproportionately benefits smaller plans; (2) endorsing or funding reference implementations 
and shared, Inferno-based test tooling that small plans can adopt rather than build; and (3) 
ensuring any conformance-testing regime (Section 10) includes a low-cost path for a small plan 
to demonstrate compliance. 
Variance across plan implementations. Plans differ widely in benefit design, delegation 
arrangements, and underlying systems, and much of that diversity is legitimate. But it also 
drives the implementation variance that, as we describe in Section 10, is today the single largest 
drag on real-world interoperability: two plans that are conformant on paper can expose APIs that 
behave differently enough to break the same application. The remedy is not to flatten plan-level 
diversity but to constrain the variance that matters for interoperability, through clear and 
prescriptive guidance, the named capability sets we discuss in Section 1.2, and the objective 
conformance testing we recommend in Section 10. We flag it here because it is the common 
thread linking the endpoint-directory, metrics, and RFI proposals. 
10.  Response to RFI: Improving Implementation of Payer API Technology 
This RFI is squarely within our experience, and we encourage CMS to act on it. The central 
problem in the ecosystem today is not the absence of standards. It is inconsistent conformance 
to them. Two payers can each claim conformance to the same IG yet expose APIs that behave 
differently enough that an app or provider integration built against one fails against the other. 
This variance is the single largest drag on real-world adoption. 
Much of this variance is semantic rather than syntactic: two payers can each produce 
structurally valid FHIR that nonetheless populates fields inconsistently, which is where most 
real-world integrations break. Shared, community-maintained reference artifacts are an effective 
way to close that gap. As one example, HealthLX has open-sourced CoCo, a canonical, 
field-level schema that maps healthcare data to FHIR for CMS use cases (cocodata.org); we 
offer it, and tools like it, as a contribution to any CMS- or HL7-coordinated reference effort, not 
as something CMS should mandate. 
We recommend CMS pursue the following: 
â€¢â€‹
Mandatory, standardized conformance testing. Require impacted payers to pass an 
objective, automated conformance test suite (for example, ONC-recognized 
Inferno-based test kits already used for FHIR testing) before attesting compliance, and 
on an ongoing basis after changes. Self-attestation without testing is the status quo and 
it has not produced consistent behavior. 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹
Page 10 of 13 
â€¢â€‹
Leverage the ONC Health IT Certification Program. We support CMS's stated interest 
in leveraging the ONC Certification Program for payer-facing API technology. A 
certification pathway for payer API technology, analogous to certified EHR technology, 
would let payers and their vendors demonstrate conformance once against a recognized 
benchmark rather than being re-tested ad hoc by every counterparty. Moreover, an 
up-front certification model shifts the industry from a reactive, audit-based posture to a 
proactive one, in which conformance is established before deployment rather than 
discovered after the fact. 
â€¢â€‹
Production monitoring and transparency. Pair pre-production testing with lightweight 
production monitoring (uptime, response conformance) and public transparency on 
results. The endpoint directory in Section II.E is a natural foundation for this: once 
endpoints are centrally known, automated conformance and availability checks become 
feasible. 
â€¢â€‹
Use the PA-API adoption metric as an oversight signal. The proposed metric for the 
percentage of prior authorization requests received through the Prior Authorization API 
(Section 5) is a ready-made oversight indicator. A payer reporting a persistently low 
share of volume through its API, even while attesting compliance, is a clear signal that its 
API is not usable in practice and warrants follow-up. We encourage CMS to use this 
metric to prioritize where conformance scrutiny is most needed. 
â€¢â€‹
Test against real-world clients. Conformance testing should include the 
app-registration and authorization flows, not just FHIR read operations, because 
registration and authorization are where integrations most often break in production. 
Recurring third-party assessments of the Patient Access API ecosystem, such as 
Flexpa's State of the Payer Patient Access API reports, which benchmark authorization, 
reliability, and conformance across hundreds of payer endpoints, document exactly this 
pattern. 
11.  Response to RFI: Increasing Health Care Resiliency (Cybersecurity) 
As the rule expands the volume and sensitivity of data flowing through payer APIs, security and 
resiliency must scale with it. We support CMS examining this and offer the following 
observations from an implementer's standpoint: 
â€¢â€‹
Standardize authentication to strengthen security at scale. The same fragmented, 
bilaterally negotiated trust model that hampers scalability (Section 1.3) also weakens 
security, because every bespoke connection is a separately managed attack surface. 
Converging on the FAST Security IG / UDAP trust-community model improves both 
interoperability and security posture by replacing ad hoc credentials with a managed, 
auditable trust framework. 
â€¢â€‹
Reduce reliance on brittle point-to-point connections. In response to CMS's 
question on point-to-point connections: the proliferation of one-off point-to-point 
integrations is both an operational fragility and a security liability. Standardized, 
directory-discoverable endpoints (Section II.E) and standardized trust frameworks 
reduce the number of bespoke connections each party must secure and monitor. 
HealthLX â€¢ Comments on CMS-0062-Pâ€‹
Page 11 of 13 
â€¢â€‹
Build in graceful degradation. Resiliency requirements should ensure that an outage 
or compromise of one participant (a payer, a clearinghouse, or a vendor) does not 
cascade. We encourage CMS to consider expectations around incident notification, 
failover, and the ability to fall back to a compliant alternative pathway without halting 
patient care. 
â€¢â€‹
Align, do not duplicate, existing frameworks. Any new resiliency or cybersecurity 
expectations should be harmonized with existing HIPAA Security Rule obligations and 
recognized frameworks (e.g., NIST) rather than creating a parallel, payer-API-specific 
regime that increases compliance complexity without adding protection. 
12.  Severability (Section I.D) 
CMS requests comment on which policies could be severable. We recommend that the 
standards-versioning and endpoint-reporting provisions (Sections II.A cross-referencing and 
II.E) be treated as severable and durable: they deliver value independent of the drug-specific 
prior-authorization proposals and should remain in force even if particular drug-PA timing 
provisions are modified. Conversely, the components that depend on less-mature IGs (CDex, 
FAST Security) should be structured so that delaying or softening them does not undermine the 
core FHIR prior-authorization workflow, which can and should proceed. 
Conclusion 
As a founding member of the HL7 Da Vinci Project and an active contributor to the reference 
implementations behind many of these standards since their inception, HealthLX commends 
CMS, HHS, and ONC for a proposed rule that meaningfully advances interoperability and 
prior-authorization reform. Our work in Da Vinci has given us a clear view both of the "north star" 
these standards are designed to reach and of the consensus-driven process required to align 
payers, providers, vendors, and regulators around a single national direction. As implementers, 
we also know firsthand what it takes to put these standards into production at scale. That 
combined perspective is why we support the direction of the rule, and why our 
recommendations focus on making it achievable in practice, including for the many impacted 
payers that must comply with limited budgets and technical staff: require the use-case IGs 
rather than overlapping base standards; build the endpoint directory on FHIR and the NDH 
Endpoint Profile; phase the least-mature components (CDex, FAST Security) appropriately; 
preserve version-transition overlap windows; and act on the API-implementation RFI with real, 
standardized conformance testing tied to the ONC Certification Program. 
Above all, we encourage CMS to pair these specific measures with a clearly articulated vision 
for the interoperability framework as a whole. This rule is one component of a multi-rule 
architecture spanning CMS-9115-F, CMS-0057-F, CMS-4208-F, the ONC Health IT Certification 
Program, HIPAA Administrative Simplification, and emerging national infrastructure; stating 
plainly how those pieces fit and sequence together, and committing to keep them aligned as the 
underlying standards mature, is what will give payers, vendors, and providers the confidence to 
invest fully rather than incrementally and defensively.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** HealthLX; submitted by Will Tesch, CEO
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Health IT vendor providing FHIR-based interoperability and prior authorization services to health plans; founding member of the HL7 Da Vinci Project; contributor to reference implementations; experience supporting CMS-9115-F, CMS-0057-F, and CMS-4208-F compliance.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

HealthLX strongly supports the proposed rule's direction, including drug prior authorization expansion, HIPAA adoption of FHIR for prior authorization, centralized endpoint reporting, and ONC-aligned standards versioning. It recommends targeted modifications to make implementation practical: require use-case-specific IGs rather than overlapping base standards, phase immature components, build a FHIR/NDH endpoint registry, preserve version transition windows, and require objective conformance testing.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 45 CFR 170.215; 45 CFR 162.923(b); HIPAA Administrative Simplification; references to CMS-9115-F, CMS-0057-F, CMS-4208-F, and CMS-0062-P.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR, Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS, CDex, FAST Security IG, SMART App Launch, Tiered OAuth, UDAP, CARIN RTPBC, PDex US Drug Formulary, NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary & Benefit, RTPB, NDH Endpoint Profile, X12N 278, X12N 270/271, HL7 Major.Minor.Patch, Inferno, TEFCA/QHIN, NIST.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Required FHIR IGs and capability scoping**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Use-case IGs already constrain base FHIR versions; naming both base FHIR and IGs creates version drift and ambiguity. Open-ended IG conformance also forces unused development.
- **Specific request:** Require use-case-specific IGs and treat base FHIR as incorporated through them; publish scoped capability sets in sub-regulatory guidance.

**Topic 2: FAST Security and CDex maturity**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** FAST Security and CDex are directionally correct but not yet mature enough for immediate mandatory adoption at scale.
- **Specific request:** Keep FAST Security and CDex recommended for now, signal intent to require later, and use production deployment, trust-community, and connectathon/test results as readiness criteria.

**Topic 3: Pharmacy benefit standards**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB align non-Part D programs with established Part D practice and serve distinct, non-duplicative functions.
- **Specific request:** Retain both F&B and RTPB; set expectations for timely F&B updates, such as weekly and promptly after prior authorization indicator changes.

**Topic 4: Medical benefit drugs and routing**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Support with clarification
- **Rationale:** Reusing CRD/DTR/PAS for medical benefit drugs avoids parallel infrastructure, but edge cases arise when a drug may be covered under either benefit.
- **Specific request:** Use claims-adjudication pathway as the default rubric, pair it with a machine-readable CRD CoverageInformation routing signal, and confirm that dual-pathway drugs can appear in both workflows without noncompliance.

**Topic 5: API endpoint reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Endpoint discovery is a major practical barrier; a centralized directory would reduce integration friction.
- **Specific request:** Use a FHIR-enabled registry aligned with the NDH Endpoint Profile; avoid redundant capability statement URL reporting; collect structured auth details; extend initial reporting to 90 days and allow 30 days for manual updates until automated reporting is available.

**Topic 6: API usage and public metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Usage metrics are essential for measuring adoption, especially the percentage of prior authorization requests received through the Prior Authorization API.
- **Specific request:** Retain PA API adoption metrics, support FHIR-based automated reporting, allow transitional portal/form reporting for small plans, and treat metrics as complementary to conformance testing.

**Topic 7: Standards versioning and expiration**
- **Provision ID:** ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support with clarification
- **Rationale:** Cross-referencing ONC-approved versions reduces lag between standards maturity and permitted use. Hard cutovers without overlap would break production integrations.
- **Specific request:** Permit compatible Minor.Patch IG versions without new rulemaking and retain at least 12-18 months of transition overlap before older versions expire.

**Topic 8: HIPAA adoption of FHIR for prior authorization**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support with limits
- **Rationale:** FHIR-based HIPAA standards align HIPAA transactions with CMS API mandates, but broad replacement of X12 eligibility is premature.
- **Specific request:** Adopt FHIR for prior-authorization-related X12N 278 and narrow 270/271 prior authorization checks, retain X12 270/271 for other eligibility uses, preserve coexistence, and phase down the direct data entry exception only after maturity is demonstrated.

**Topic 9: Small plans, vendors, PBMs, and delegated entities**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Payers depend on PBMs, delegated entities, and vendors for data and operations; small plans have limited technical capacity.
- **Specific request:** Confirm compliance can be achieved through vendors/delegates, require data holders such as PBMs to support standards, allow accommodations for delegated-entity readiness gaps, support aggregated vendor submissions, and fund reference implementations and low-cost test tooling.

**Topic 10: Payer API implementation RFI and conformance**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; API-USAGE-METRICS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The main barrier is inconsistent conformance, including semantic variance, not lack of standards.
- **Specific request:** Require standardized automated conformance testing, leverage ONC Certification, monitor production availability/conformance, use PA API adoption metrics as oversight signals, and test registration/authorization flows against real-world clients.

**Topic 11: Cybersecurity and resiliency RFI**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support with clarification
- **Rationale:** Expanded API data exchange increases security and resiliency stakes.
- **Specific request:** Standardize authentication through FAST/UDAP over time, reduce one-off point-to-point connections, require graceful degradation and incident expectations, and align new requirements with HIPAA Security Rule and NIST rather than creating duplicative regimes.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** Supports requiring use-case-specific IGs while treating base FHIR as incorporated through those IGs, to avoid duplicate and conflicting requirements.
- **S2/S3:** Supports ONC cross-referencing and later compatible Minor.Patch versions, with clear transition windows for version changes.
- **S6:** Discusses CARIN RTPBC and PDex Drug Formulary as complementary; supports recommending RTPBC for Patient Access where PBM data dependencies are considered.
- **S12:** Supports adding medical-benefit drugs to the Prior Authorization API and says the October 1, 2027 date is achievable if the final rule is timely.
- **S14:** Supports applying NCPDP pharmacy benefit standards beyond Part D because they extend a proven baseline.
- **S15:** Recommends claims-adjudication pathway as the primary medical/pharmacy benefit rubric, supported by machine-readable CRD routing signals and guidance for edge cases.
- **S19:** Notes Medicaid/CHIP and non-Part D readiness depends partly on PBMs and delegated entities; asks CMS to account for those dependencies.
- **S21:** Says the 2027 timeline is achievable for extensions of existing CMS-0057-F workflows but risky for less-mature components or delayed finalization.
- **S22:** Says F&B and RTPB have distinct value and should both be retained, while CMS should define F&B update latency expectations.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports centralized endpoint reporting through a FHIR-enabled, NDH-aligned registry, with structured auth details, less redundant data, 90-day initial reporting, and flexible update paths.
- **S25:** Treats RTPB as valuable and distinct from F&B, especially for real-time patient-specific coverage and cost.
- **S28:** Supports alignment with existing Part D/NCPDP practice rather than building a new pharmacy benefit pathway.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Supports API usage metrics, especially PA API adoption rate, and recommends automated FHIR-based reporting with transitional portal/form options.
- **S31:** Addresses QHP/small plan needs indirectly by supporting transitional reporting paths and accommodations for smaller plans.
- **S37:** Identifies implementation challenges from immature IGs, inconsistent conformance, delegated entities, and semantic variance.
- **S40/S41/S42:** Says FF-SHOP issuers can largely reuse individual-market QHP API implementations and that January 1, 2028 provides reasonable runway.
- **S44:** Supports FHIR as appropriate for prior-authorization-specific HIPAA transactions.
- **S45:** Supports a narrow scope covering referral certification/authorization and the prior-authorization subset of eligibility, not wholesale eligibility replacement.
- **S46:** Recommends X12 coexistence, especially retaining X12N 270/271 for non-prior-authorization eligibility uses.
- **S47/S53:** Supports 24/36-month HIPAA timelines and phased implementation for less mature components.
- **S48/S49:** Notes cost and burden implications for small health plans and recommends low-cost testing and reference implementations.
- **S50:** Identifies FAST Security and CDex as not yet mature enough for immediate mandates.
- **S51:** Notes non-CMS covered entities, providers, clearinghouses, and small/rural practices are earlier in their FHIR journey and need time.
- **S54/S55:** Recommends objective conformance testing, certification, production monitoring, and oversight using usage metrics.
- **S60/S61/S63/S64/S65:** Supports ONC-aligned versioning, compatible Minor.Patch flexibility, stakeholder coordination, and transition periods for version expiration.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to general RFIs on payer API implementation and resiliency by recommending conformance testing, ONC certification, endpoint-based monitoring, FAST/UDAP trust, reduced point-to-point reliance, and alignment with existing security frameworks.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Require use-case-specific IGs and treat base FHIR versions as incorporated through those IGs.
2. Scope required IG capabilities by use case and publish capability sets in refreshable guidance.
3. Keep FAST Security and CDex recommended until production maturity, trust infrastructure, and testing support mandatory use.
4. Retain NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB for pharmacy benefit drugs and define F&B update latency expectations.
5. Use CRD CoverageInformation to route drugs between FHIR medical benefit and NCPDP pharmacy benefit workflows.
6. Build endpoint reporting as a FHIR-enabled registry aligned with the NDH Endpoint Profile.
7. Remove redundant capability-statement URL reporting and collect structured authentication details.
8. Extend initial endpoint reporting to 90 days and provide a longer manual-update window while automated reporting matures.
9. Support FHIR-based automated API usage metric reporting with transitional portal/form options.
10. Preserve standards version transition overlap and allow compatible Minor.Patch updates without new rulemaking.
11. Adopt FHIR under HIPAA only for prior-authorization-related referral/authorization and narrow eligibility checks, while preserving X12 for other eligibility transactions.
12. Require standardized conformance testing, leverage ONC Certification, and monitor production API availability and conformance.
13. Recognize vendors, PBMs, and delegated entities in compliance, reporting, and enforcement models.
14. Provide small-plan support through reference implementations, shared test tools, and low-cost compliance paths.
15. Align cybersecurity/resiliency expectations with HIPAA Security Rule and NIST.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Version drift from separately requiring base FHIR and IGs; immature FAST Security/CDex mandates; endpoint discovery friction; inconsistent payer API conformance; delegated-entity/PBM dependencies; small plan burden; overly broad replacement of X12 eligibility.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Broken production integrations, duplicated development, delayed patient/provider access, burden shifted to providers through portals, compliance exposure for plans that depend on unready vendors or PBMs, and fragile cybersecurity from bespoke point-to-point connections.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Lack of scalable trust communities, limited production maturity for some IGs, manual endpoint reporting, inconsistent semantic mapping, PBM data dependencies, small-plan resource limits, and insufficient conformance testing.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No quantitative statistics are provided.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Flexpa State of the Payer Patient Access API reports are referenced as evidence of authorization, reliability, and conformance problems across payer endpoints.
- **Examples provided:** HealthLX cites its own payer implementation experience, Da Vinci participation, open-source CoCo mapping schema, recurring F&B file latency issues, and common integration failures from payer-to-payer API variance.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Impacted payers, small health plans, MA organizations, Medicaid/CHIP programs, QHP issuers, PBMs, providers, EHR vendors, app developers, clearinghouses, technology vendors, patients, CMS, HHS, ONC, HL7, and NCPDP.
- **Economic implications:** Recommendations aim to reduce duplicative builds, redundant reporting, manual integration costs, and small-plan burden, while recognizing that conformance testing and standards support require investment.
- **Technical feasibility:** The core drug PA extensions are feasible if built on existing CMS-0057-F workflows; CDex, FAST Security, and broad FHIR HIPAA adoption require phasing and maturity checks.
- **Patient care impact:** Better endpoint discovery, prior authorization APIs, and conformance testing should reduce delays, improve access to drug PA information, and make APIs usable in practice.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We are in strong support of the overall direction of this proposed rule." - Context: Opening summary of HealthLX's overall position.
2. "We recommend that CMS require the use-case-specific IGs and treat the base FHIR standard as incorporated by reference through those IGs." - Context: Recommendation on FHIR-IG-REQUIRED implementation.
3. "Endpoint discovery is one of the largest practical barriers to interoperability today." - Context: Support for API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING.
4. "The central problem in the ecosystem today is not the absence of standards. It is inconsistent conformance to them." - Context: Response to the payer API implementation RFI.
